subject: Geography
title: Advanced Mapwork and Interpretation
outline: Revision of scale, distance and area
Scale changes resulting from reduction and enlargement
Cross-sections, gradient and vertical exaggeration revisited
Interpretation of relief, drainage and landuse
Relationship between physical features and human activities

modules.title: Map Reduction and Enlargement
modules.html:
Principles

Reduction means redrawing a map to a smaller size; enlargement means redrawing it to a larger size. In both cases the shape and relative positions of features must remain the same, and the scale must be adjusted.

The Square (Grid) Method

  1. Draw a grid of squares over the original map (or use the existing grid).
  2. Draw a second grid with the same number of squares, but with each side multiplied by the enlargement factor \(n\) or divided by the reduction factor.
  3. Copy the detail square by square, keeping relative positions.
  4. Add a title, key, north arrow and the new scale.

New Scale After Reduction or Enlargement

If the original R.F. is \(1:D\):

$$\text{Enlargement } n \text{ times} \Rightarrow \text{New R.F.} = 1:\frac{D}{n}$$ $$\text{Reduction to } \frac{1}{n} \Rightarrow \text{New R.F.} = 1:(D\times n)$$

Note that enlargement gives a larger scale (smaller denominator) and reduction gives a smaller scale. The new linear scale must always be drawn on the new map.

Effect on Area

Because area is two-dimensional, enlarging a map \(n\) times increases its area by \(n^{2}\), while reducing it to \(1/n\) reduces its area to \(1/n^{2}\). The ground area represented, however, does not change.

Percentage Changes

An enlargement of 50% means each linear dimension becomes \(1.5\) times the original, so the factor is \(n=1.5\); a reduction of 25% means each dimension becomes \(0.75\) of the original, so \(D\) is divided by 0.75, i.e. multiplied by \(\tfrac{4}{3}\).

examples.q: A map of scale 1:50,000 is enlarged three times. State the new scale and the effect on the area of the drawing.
examples.a: New R.F. \(= 1:\dfrac{50{,}000}{3} = 1{:}16{,}667\) (approximately). Each linear dimension becomes three times as long, so the area of the drawing becomes \(3^{2}=9\) times the original, although the ground area represented remains unchanged.

examples.q: A map drawn to a scale of 1:25,000 is reduced to half its size. Determine the new scale and the statement scale.
examples.a: Reduction by half means the denominator is doubled: New R.F. \(= 1:(25{,}000\times2) = 1{:}50{,}000\). Statement scale: \(\dfrac{50{,}000}{100{,}000} = 0.5\), so 1 cm now represents 0.5 km.

modules.title: Map Interpretation: Relief, Drainage and Landuse
modules.html:
Systematic Description

A good interpretation answers four questions about each element: what is present, where it is (use grid references and compass directions), how much (heights, distances, areas), and why (the relationship between features).

Relief Description

State the general relief type (highland, lowland, undulating plain, plateau), the highest and lowest heights with grid references, the amplitude of relief (highest minus lowest), the direction of slope, and the specific features - ridges, escarpments, spurs, valleys, cols, conical hills, flood plains.

Drainage Description

Name the main river and its tributaries, state the direction of flow with evidence, describe the drainage pattern and density, and mention associated features such as rapids, waterfalls, swamps, lakes, meanders, ox-bow lakes or a delta.

Landuse and Settlement

  • Landuse: farmland, plantations, forest reserve, grazing land, quarry, mining, built-up area, recreation.
  • Settlement: pattern (nucleated, dispersed, linear), size hierarchy, site (wet point, dry point, bridge point, nodal, defensive) and functions suggested by symbols such as market, school, post office, dispensary or police station.
  • Communication: main and minor roads, railways, footpaths, bridges, ferries and airstrips, noting how routes avoid steep slopes and swamps and converge on nodal towns.

Relationships

Physical factorHuman response
Steep slopes and highlandsSparse settlement, forestry, grazing, terracing, winding roads
Flood plains and swampsRice farming and fishing; settlement avoided or built on levees
River confluences and bridge pointsGrowth of nucleated market towns and route centres
Waterfalls and narrow valleysDam and HEP sites
Mineral depositsQuarries, mining settlements and access roads

Examination Technique

  1. Read the scale, contour interval and key before answering.
  2. Support every statement with evidence: grid references, heights, distances and directions.
  3. Use neat, labelled sketch maps and sections with a title and scale.
  4. Show all working in calculations of distance, area, gradient and vertical exaggeration, and give the correct units.

examples.q: A map of scale 1:50,000 shows a proposed dam site. Give three pieces of map evidence that would justify the choice of site.
examples.a: (i) A narrow, steep-sided valley or gorge shown by closely spaced contours, which shortens and cheapens the dam wall; (ii) a wide, gently sloping basin upstream indicated by widely spaced contours, giving a large reservoir capacity; (iii) a river with a large catchment and steady flow, plus a waterfall or rapids showing a good head of water for power generation, with few settlements to be resettled in the flooded area.

examples.q: On a 1:50,000 map two towns are 9.6 cm apart by road. A vehicle travels at an average speed of 40 km per hour. How long will the journey take?
examples.a: Ground distance \(= 9.6 \times 0.5 = 4.8\text{ km}\). Time \(= \dfrac{4.8}{40} = 0.12\) hours \(= 0.12\times60 = 7.2\) minutes, i.e. about 7 minutes 12 seconds.

quiz.q: When a map is enlarged twice, the new scale of a 1:50,000 map becomes
quiz.solution: Enlargement divides the denominator by the factor: 50,000/2 = 25,000.

quiz.q: Reducing a 1:25,000 map to one-quarter of its size gives a new scale of
Enlarging a map three times increases the area of the drawing by a factor of
quiz.solution: Area varies as the square of the linear factor, so 3 squared = 9.

quiz.q: Which of the following remains unchanged when a map is reduced?
options: Length of the linear scale bar
quiz.solution: Only the drawing and its scale change; the actual ground area is fixed.

quiz.q: The most suitable method of enlarging a map is the
quiz.solution: Corresponding squares keep the shape and relative positions accurate.

quiz.q: A new map produced by enlargement must always carry
quiz.solution: Failure to redraw the scale makes all measurements wrong.

quiz.q: On a 1:50,000 map, a road measuring 12 cm represents a ground distance of
quiz.solution: 1 cm represents 0.5 km, so 12 x 0.5 = 6 km.

quiz.q: A journey of 6 km at an average speed of 30 km/h will take
The difference between the highest and the lowest point on a map is called the
quiz.solution: Amplitude of relief measures the total range of height.

quiz.q: Which map evidence best suggests a settlement is a route centre?
options: It has a river beside it
quiz.solution: Converging roads and railways identify a nodal or route centre.

quiz.q: A quarry symbol close to a cement factory on a map suggests
quiz.solution: Raw-material orientation locates cement plants beside limestone quarries.

quiz.q: Rice cultivation is most likely to be found on the map in
options: seasonally flooded plains and swampy valleys
quiz.solution: Padi rice needs level land that holds water.

quiz.q: Settlements are usually avoided on flood plains because of
quiz.solution: Regular inundation makes building risky and unhealthy.

quiz.q: A good dam site on a map is indicated by
options: a wide flat valley with dispersed towns
a narrow gorge with a broad basin upstream
quiz.solution: A narrow gorge reduces construction cost while the basin stores water.

quiz.q: In map interpretation, statements should always be supported with
quiz.solution: Evidence from the map earns the marks in WAEC and NECO questions.

quiz.q: If the vertical scale is 1 cm to 50 m and the horizontal scale is 1:50,000, the vertical exaggeration is
Roads in a hilly area on a map are usually winding because they
options: avoid steep gradients by following contours
quiz.solution: Zig-zag routes reduce the gradient that vehicles must climb.
